title: Supreme Court declines Trump push to cut research grants related to DEI | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The Supreme Court declined on Monday to take up an appeal from the Trump administration defending its decision to cancel tens of millions of dollars in grants to University of California researchers because their work touched on diversity, equity and inclusion — allowing the money to flow the school.

At stake was about $150 million in National Science Foundation andNational Endowment for the Humanitiesgrants that President Donald Trump attempted to cancel shortly after taking office, part of the administration’s broader campaign to attack any initiative focused on diversity. Billions of dollars in research grants to other entities have also been caught up in litigation that could eventually reach the Supreme Court.

The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals concluded that canceling the grants likely violated the First Amendment and the Trump administration appealed to the high court in August. By declining to take the appeal, the Supreme Court left in place a ruling that requires the administration to fund the grants related to DEI and allowed these cases to proceed in federal district courts (rather than the specialized federal claims court).

“The government can point to no case where this court, or any court, has held that the president and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the California researchers told the high court.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, framed the debate as a shift in priorities for federal funding that he said did not implicate the First Amendment.

The First Amendment, the Justice Department argued in its appeal, “does not prohibit the government from declining to award competitive grants that fund research projects that promote DEI.”

“In addition to leaving intact the lower courts’ ruling for the researchers, the denial is also significant in at least tacitly endorsing the lower courts’ conclusion that these kinds of disputes properly belong in federal district courts, rather than the specialized federal claims court,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center.

“That may seem like an incredibly technical distinction, but the claims court can only issue narrow, limited relief against the government at the end of the case, whereas district courts, as in this case, can move much faster and much more coercively to restore funds that were wrongly cut off.”

As is usually the case, the Supreme Court did not explain its decision to deny the appeal. There were no dissents.
